_comment: THE CLOSED SET of encodings a chain's identifiers may be DECLARED in, and the closed set
of identifier KINDS a declaration may speak about. Configuration.md §2.1 (the registry
schema) and §2.2 (the additive rule); Search-And-Routing.md §2 is where every member
comes from.
── WHAT THIS IS FOR, AND WHAT READS IT NOW: SHARD-PATH DERIVATION ──────────────────────
The requirement is that an identifier's encoding is a property of the chain, carried as
DATA in the published registry, rather than the `0x` + hex assumption baked into every
path, shard key and index. This file defines the DECLARATION — the closed set a chain may
draw its per-kind tokens from — and, since the derivation step landed, the RULE each
member implies for a shard path segment (`shardKey` below).
SHARD DERIVATION READS `chains[<slug>].identifierEncoding`.
`src/blocktracer/contract/shards.nim` takes the encoding as a parameter —
`shardKeyFor(encoding, identifier)` — and reads its rule out of THIS FILE, so there is no
second table of per-encoding behaviour anywhere. `src/blocktracer_client/paths.nim`
re-exports that one function, so the producer, the validator and the browser derive one
way. The producers hand it the same value they publish; the client and the validator read
it back out of the registry.
TWO SITES STILL DERIVE FROM THE STRING, and both are deliberately later steps:
the hash index      `src/blocktracer/contract/hashshard.nim` — `hexToBytes` parses hex
pairs and `stripHex` lowercases unconditionally. This is a
PUBLISHED self-describing wire format, so widening it is a
migration of every published shard plus a compatibility window
(Publishing-And-Caching.md §6.1, §6.2) and must land alone.
the capture tooling `tools/capture/lib/entities.mjs` filters published directory
entries on a literal `0x` at two sites. It reads the tree the hash
index keys, so it follows the index rather than the derivation:
a filter widened ahead of the index would enumerate entities the
index cannot key.
CASE HANDLING IS ALSO STILL GLOBAL and is the step between those two — see the section
on it below. `shardKeyFor` normalises NOTHING, which is why the derivation could land
first: it slices, and a slice of a case-significant identifier keeps its case.
THE DECLARATION LANDED FIRST ON PURPOSE, and the derivation second for the same reason.
Before a non-hex chain publishes, the key layout is a decision; afterwards it is a
migration of every published shard, index and URL.
── WHY THIS IS DATA AND NOT AN ENUM IN ONE LANGUAGE ───────────────────────────────────
For the reason `refusal-reasons.json` and `snapshot-format.json` beside it are data. The
two registry PRODUCERS are both Nim today — `src/blocktracer/chain/ingest.nim` and
`src/blocktracer/demo/generator.nim` — so one Nim enum would close the set for them. It
would not close it for the tooling that has to agree with them: the capture tooling is
JavaScript and is one of the derivation sites named above, so the moment anything
consumes the declaration the set is needed in both languages, and a set that is closed in
one and open in the other is not closed.
`src/blocktracer/contract/identifier_encoding.nim` reads this file with `staticRead` at
COMPILE time, so a member added here is a member there with nobody remembering to copy
it, and a file that is missing or malformed fails the BUILD rather than producing a
producer that writes whatever it likes. `tools/chain/identifier-encoding-selftest.mjs` is
the JavaScript side's live read: it is a test rather than a consumer for now — the one site
that will make it a consumer is the capture tooling, which follows the hash index — but it
means the JavaScript half of this file is EXERCISED rather than declared correct for later.
── `shardKey`: WHAT EACH MEMBER IMPLIES FOR A PATH SEGMENT ─────────────────────────────
A shard path segment is the leading FOUR characters of the identifier's PAYLOAD, in the
identifier's own alphabet (Static-Site-Architecture.md §2's `{h0h1}` / `{a0a1}`: the first
two bytes, which for hex is four characters). Four fields say how to get there, and they
are here rather than in Nim so that the set and the behaviour of its members cannot
disagree — a member added without a rule fails the BUILD, because the reader requires one.
stripPrefix       a literal prefix that is NOT part of the payload's alphabet and is
removed before slicing. `0x` for hex; empty for everything else. It is
stripped only if present, so an identifier written without it shards
the same way.
payloadAfterLast  a SEPARATOR after whose last occurrence the payload begins; empty when
the whole identifier is payload. Only bech32 and bech32m use it, and
the reason is entropy rather than tidiness: a bech32 string is
`<hrp>1<data>`, so every Cardano address begins `addr` and every Fuel
address begins `fuel` — sharding on the raw leading characters would
put a whole chain in ONE bucket. `1` is the separator and is excluded
from the data charset by BIP-173, so its last occurrence is
unambiguous.
pad               the alphabet's ZERO DIGIT, used to right-pad an identifier shorter
than four payload characters so that a shard segment is always four
characters wide. Per alphabet, because `0` is not a digit of base58,
of bech32 or of base64: padding with a character the alphabet does not
contain would make a shard name that no identifier could produce.
pathSafe          whether EVERY character of the alphabet is legal inside a single path
segment. False for exactly one member — `base64`, whose alphabet
contains `/` — and the derivation REFUSES a shard key for a member
that is not path-safe rather than emitting a segment with a separator
in it. See the note on base64 below.
WHAT THESE FIELDS DELIBERATELY DO NOT SAY IS ANYTHING ABOUT CASE. `shardKeyFor` slices and
pads; it does not normalise, so a base58 or base64url key keeps its case for free. The
hash index's `stripHex`, one module over, still lowercases unconditionally, and fixing that
per encoding is the next step rather than this one — keeping them apart is what let the
derivation land with the published hex layout asserted byte-for-byte unchanged.
BASE64 IS DECLARABLE AND NOT SHARDABLE, and that pair is the honest state rather than an
oversight. TON's transaction hashes and Sui's digests really are base64 (§2 row 8), so the
registry has to be able to SAY so; but the standard base64 alphabet contains `/` and `+`,
and roughly one in eight 44-character digests carries one in its first four characters. A
derivation that worked for seven digests in eight and silently created a nested directory
for the eighth is worse than one that refuses, so `shardKeyFor` refuses `base64` outright.
Choosing the path-safe re-encoding that would close it (base64url of the same bytes? the
hex of the decoded digest?) is a decision Search-And-Routing.md §2 and §5 do not make, and
making it here would be amending the spec from a data file. It is recorded, like the
`aleo1…` gap below, rather than quietly filled — and it is the reason TON and Move stay
gated.
── WHY THE VALUE IS PER KIND AND NOT ONE TOKEN PER CHAIN ──────────────────────────────
Because a single per-chain token is measurably too narrow, on three of the chains whose
publication this seam gates. Search-And-Routing.md §2's shape table gives:
TON          addresses are base64url, 48 characters with an `EQ`/`UQ`/`kQ` prefix;
transaction hashes are base64, 44. Two non-hex encodings, differing from
each other, on one chain, and §2 names both outright.
Fuel         addresses are bech32m `fuel1…`; transaction hashes are `0x` + 64 hex. §2
lists FuelVM in both rows.
Move / Sui   a DIGEST is base64, 44 characters, per §2.
TON OR FUEL ALONE SETTLES THE SHAPE, and the Sui row is cited more carefully than the
other two because §2 does not in fact supply its address half. §2's `0x` + 64 hex row is
labelled `transaction hash · block hash` and lists Move among its families; it gives Move
no ADDRESS row at all. So `Sui addresses are 0x + 64 hex` is the Move charter's statement
— Recorders/Recorder-Move.milestones.org, which says they `resolve under the existing
assumption` — and not row 2's. Reading an address claim out of a row labelled for hashes
would be the same amendment-by-inference as filling the `aleo1…` row from this file, which
is refused below. The consequence that charter draws is unaffected: a visitor can reach a
Sui address and cannot reach a Sui transaction by its digest.
Solana is the counter-example that shows a token would have been enough for SOME chains —
both its addresses (43–44) and its signatures (87–88) are base58, differing only in
length. A shape that is right for Solana and wrong for Sui, TON and Fuel is the wrong
shape, and discovering that after a chain publishes costs a migration.
They are the chain-supplied identifiers that appear as path segments in
`src/blocktracer_client/paths.nim`, which is the one module on the consumer side that
builds every path this package reads:
transaction  `txFactsPath`, `txStatePath`, `traceSelectionPath` — sharded
address      `addressIndexPath`, `addressSegmentPath` — sharded
block        `blockPath` — content-addressed, not sharded
`traceArtifactId`, `codeHash` and `bundleHash` are deliberately NOT kinds. They are OUR
identifiers — derived by `src/blocktracer/contract/ids.nim` and hashed by us — so their
encoding is a property of this pipeline and not of any chain, and putting them here would
invite a producer to declare something about them that a chain could contradict.
A KIND MAY BE OMITTED, and omission is not a default. Static-Site-Architecture.md §2.3's
identity union exists because transaction identity is not universally a hash: Substrate is
`{ kind: "blockIndex" }`, a pair rather than an encoded string, and no member here can
honestly describe it. Omitting the kind says so; inventing a token for it would not.
AN OMITTED KIND AND AN ABSENT DECLARATION ARE NOW DISTINGUISHABLE, and the derivation
treats them differently on purpose. Asking for a kind the row OMITTED raises, naming the
kind: a producer building a sharded path for an identifier it declared it cannot describe
is a producer bug, and hex-by-default there is exactly the silent wrong answer this seam
exists to remove. A row with NO `identifierEncoding` AT ALL is a different fact — it is a
tree published before the member existed — and derives hex as a named compatibility
fallback (Publishing-And-Caching.md §6.1), from ONE function, `declaredOrLegacy`, which is
the only place in the tree that turns an absence into a token.
CASE HANDLING. It is stated per encoding — lowercasing is the right key for hex and
DESTROYS base58 and base64url, which are case-significant; bech32 and bech32m require a
uniform case rather than an arbitrary one; and an EIP-55 hex address carries its checksum
in its case, so its display form and its key form are two different strings. That is a
separate requirement with its own consumers, and a `caseSignificant` field added here now
would be a second unread declaration rather than a fix. Aztec, incidentally, needs none of
it for the kinds above: those identifiers are field elements, measured all-lowercase across
both committed captures (see `hex` below for the counts and where to re-run them).
PER-CHAIN ASSIGNMENT. Which chain uses which encoding is not in this file, because at
consumption time the published registry IS that answer — declaring it here as well would
be the second source this file exists to prevent. The producers declare it for the chains
they publish, through `identifier_encoding.nim`, which is what keeps the tokens they use
drawn from the set below.
── ONE ROW OF THE SHAPE TABLE HAS NO MEMBER HERE, AND THAT IS NOT AN OMISSION ─────────
Search-And-Routing.md §2's `aleo1…` row names a PREFIX and no encoding. `aleo1…` is in
fact bech32m, but the table does not say so, and adding a member on that basis would be
amending the spec from a data file. Aleo is also the one chain of the seven the shape
table implies that is left unchartered, so nothing is blocked by the gap. It is recorded
rather than quietly filled.
The rows the table has that are NOT identifier encodings, and therefore correctly absent:
the name suffixes (`*.eth`, `*.sol`, …), another explorer's URL, and `anything else`.
Those are inputs that RESOLVE TO an identifier; they are not a way of writing one.

encodings.shapeRows: `0x` + 64 hex (transaction hash · block hash; EVM, Starknet, Fuel, Move); `0x` + 40 hex (account or contract address; EVM); `0x` + 1-63 hex (Starknet felt)
encodings.measured: Aztec, and stated so it can be re-run. Every `0x`-hex literal in both committed captures is LOWERCASE: 386 distinct in `fixtures/chain-artifacts/aztec-testnet/`, 990 in `tests/fixtures/chain-snapshots/aztec-mainnet-live/`, with ZERO uppercase hex digits in either — transaction hashes, block hashes, contract addresses, contract class ids and artifact hashes alike. Exactly two lengths occur and both are hex: 66 (`0x` + 64, the field elements — every identifier of the three kinds above) and 42 (`0x` + 40 — `coinbase` and `rollupAddress`, L1 addresses carried as block metadata, not path segments, so no kind declares them). The demo generator's synthetic addresses are `0x` + 40 lowercase hex. So `hex` is what is true of every chain this tree publishes, rather than what was assumed of them.

shardKey.note: THE PUBLISHED LAYOUT, AND THE ONE RULE THAT MAY NOT MOVE. Every shard path Aztec has already published was derived by stripping `0x` and right-padding with `0` to four characters, so these three values are load-bearing for anything already on a CDN (Publishing-And-Caching.md §6.1). The padding looks like a curiosity and is not: without it a one-character Starknet felt would name a one-character shard directory, and `0x` + 1-63 hex is a real row of the shape table.

encodings.shapeRows: base58, 43-44 chars (Solana account or program address); base58, 87-88 chars (Solana transaction signature)

shardKey.note: The whole string is payload — base58 carries no prefix and no separator, and Solana's addresses and signatures differ only in length. `1` is base58's zero digit; `0` is not in the alphabet at all, which is why the pad is per-encoding.

encodings.shapeRows: base64, 44 chars (TON transaction hash · Sui digest)

shardKey.note: THE ONE MEMBER THAT IS DECLARABLE AND NOT SHARDABLE. The standard alphabet's 63rd and 64th digits are `+` and `/`, and `/` ends a path segment — so about one 44-character digest in eight would silently publish into a nested directory. The derivation refuses rather than doing that; the header section on base64 records why choosing the path-safe re-encoding is not this file's decision to make.

base64url exists precisely because `-` and `_` replace `+` and `/`, so every digit is legal in a path segment. The `EQ`/`UQ`/`kQ` prefix is NOT stripped: it is base64url of the address's real leading bits (the flag byte and workchain), so it is payload rather than decoration, and stripping it would make two genuinely different addresses shard alike.

`<hrp>1<data>`, so the payload begins after the LAST `1` — BIP-173 excludes `1` from the data charset, which is what makes `last` unambiguous. Sharding the raw string would key every Cardano address under `addr` and every stake address under `stak`: one bucket per address type for a whole chain. `q` is the data charset's zero digit.

Same rule as bech32, for the same reason: every Fuel address begins `fuel`. bech32m differs from bech32 only in the checksum constant, which the shard key never inspects — so the two members have the same derivation and are still separate members, because an address valid under one is invalid under the other and a consumer that validates has to know which.

SS58 is base58 of a network prefix followed by the account bytes, so the alphabet and the pad are base58's and the whole string is payload. The first character or two encode the network, which costs some entropy in the leading shard characters; that is a distribution property of the chain's own address format and not something the derivation may quietly correct.

encodings.shapeRows: decimal integer (block number · slot · checkpoint), the table's first row and the only one that is not a string of digits-plus-alphabet. It is a member because a chain whose blocks are identified by number rather than by hash — Sui's checkpoints, for one — has to be able to say so without borrowing `hex`.

shardKey.note: A rule is carried even though no kind that a decimal identifier can fill is sharded: `block` is the only kind a chain would declare `decimal` for and `blockPath` is content-addressed rather than sharded. The rule is here because the reader REQUIRES one per member — a member with no rule fails the build — and because a member whose rule was omitted on the grounds that nothing reaches it is a member that derives nothing the first time something does. Leading decimal digits shard badly (every block in a range shares them); a chain that needed a well-distributed key for a number would be declaring the wrong thing about it.
